title: Spin Chain Quantum Communication on a Trapped-Ion Processor
authors: Madhumita Sarkar, Trinity Pointon, Sougato Bose
abstract: Efficient communication between distant qubits is one of the central challenges in scaling quantum processors. Although engineered spin chain protocols have been extensively investigated theoretically, their experimental realization has remained comparatively limited. Here, we experimentally realize engineered quantum communication protocols through digitally simulated spin Hamiltonian on IonQ's Forte 1/ Forte Enterprise 1 trapped-ion quantum processor. Combining exact numerical simulations with quantum hardware experiments, we benchmark uniform nearest-neighbour and engineered coupling profiles and demonstrate that engineered interactions significantly enhance the fidelity of quantum state transfer. We further show that exploiting the commutation structure of the spin Hamiltonian enables a parallel Trotter decomposition that more faithfully reproduces the target dynamics while substantially reducing the circuit depth and execution time compared to the conventional sequential implementations. Our results demonstrate that programmable quantum processors can effectively realize and efficiently implement quantum communication protocols, bringing Hamiltonian-based quantum communication closer to practical quantum technologies.
summary: The authors experimentally demonstrate high-fidelity quantum state transfer across a spin chain using trapped-ion processors. They show that engineering the qubit couplings significantly outperforms simple nearest-neighbor interactions. Crucially, they also optimize the gate implementation by using parallel Trotterization, making Hamiltonian-based communication more practical for real quantum hardware.
main_problem: The central challenge addressed is achieving efficient, high-fidelity quantum communication between distant qubits necessary for scaling quantum processors.
main_result: Engineered coupling profiles significantly enhance the fidelity of quantum state transfer compared to uniform nearest-neighbor couplings. Furthermore, exploiting Hamiltonian commutation structure allows for a parallel Trotter decomposition that reduces circuit depth and execution time.
method: The research combines exact numerical simulations with experimental measurements performed on a trapped-ion quantum processor using gate-based quantum simulation techniques (Trotterization).
model_or_system: The system models a one-dimensional spin chain governed by an XY Hamiltonian, $H = \sum J_{ij} (X_i X_j + Y_i Y_j)$. The physical platform utilized is IonQ's trapped-ion quantum processor.
key_observables: State Transfer Fidelity ($F(t)$), coherence preservation ($\langle Z_{N-1} angle$), circuit depth, and execution time.
important_parameters: Coupling strengths ($J_{ij}$), chain length ($N$), Trotter step size ($\Delta t$), and the comparison between uniform vs. engineered coupling profiles (e.g., $J_j \propto j(N-j)$).
main_assumptions: The primary approximations involve using the first-order Lie-Trotter product formula to simulate continuous time evolution on a discrete gate-based processor, and acknowledging that observed fidelity drops are due to hardware errors.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate quantum state transfer dynamics, comparing engineered vs. uniform couplings (Fig 4), showing population evolution for both single excitations and superpositions (Figs 6 & 7), and detailing the comparison between sequential and parallel Trotter implementations (Fig 5).
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares different protocols: first, demonstrating state transfer using nearest-neighbor couplings; second, proving that engineered coupling profiles enhance fidelity; third, optimizing the implementation by showing that parallel decomposition reduces circuit depth compared to serial methods.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges theoretical quantum information concepts (Hamiltonian dynamics, PST) with cutting-edge experimental hardware (trapped ions), providing concrete benchmarks for scalable quantum networking protocols.

A quantum state initially en- coded in the leftmost qubit, propagates coherently through the chain under the engineered nearest-neighbour couplings Ji and is reconstructed at the opposite end after the opti- mal transfer time. (b) Digital implementation of the corre- sponding nearest-neighbour XY Hamiltonian on the trapped- ion quantum processor. The continuous Hamiltonian evolu- tion is approximated using a first-order Trotter decomposi- tion, in which each Trotter step is realized through a sequence of experimentally accessible two-qubit interactions and single qubit rotations.

FIG. 2. Convergence of the gate-based Trotter approximation towards the exact NN dynamics with increasing numbers of Trotter steps for (a) N = 3, and (b) N = 5. As the number of Trotter steps increases, the gate-based evolution approaches the exact Hamiltonian evolution.

FIG. 3. Experimental state-transfer fidelity (red circles) as a function of time for NN spin chains with uniform coupling strength J = −1, compared with the corresponding gate-based simulations (green dashed lines) and exact Hamiltonian evolution (blue solid lines) for (a) N = 3, (b) N = 4, and (c) N = 5. As the chain length increases, the fidelity peak shifts to later times while its maximum value decreases, reflecting the increasing challenge of coherent state transfer over longer spin chains. Nevertheless, the measured fidelities remain above the classical threshold of 2/3 for all system sizes investigated, demonstrating a quantum advantage.
